set1.q: A 55-year-old woman with cirrhosis takes a diuretic, is anxious and has low albumin. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.58 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 34 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 31 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 135 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 93 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). From a baseline carbon dioxide of 40 mm Hg and bicarbonate of 25 mEq/L, in metabolic alkalosis carbon dioxide rises 0.75 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L rise in bicarbonate. Which part of her history best explains the metabolic alkalosis?
opts: Her anxiety

Anxiety causes hyperventilation and explains the respiratory alkalosis, the low carbon dioxide of 34. It does not raise bicarbonate. Tell: the metabolic side needs a bicarbonate-raising cause, the diuretic.
adjacent fact
Her low albumin
Low albumin lowers the measured anion gap and calls for correcting it; it is not a listed cause of metabolic alkalosis. Tell: low albumin changes the gap calculation.
confused mechanism or drug class
Her liver disease alone

Liver disease is part of the listed setting, but the cause of metabolic alkalosis in that pair is the diuretic, which drives sodium reabsorption with hydrogen secretion. Tell: look for a listed alkalosis cause, such as a diuretic, vomiting or suction.
competing diagnosis
Her diuretic

Correct. Bicarbonate 31 with pH 7.58 is a metabolic alkalosis; expected carbon dioxide = 40 + 0.75 x 6 = 44.5, but hers is 34, so a respiratory alkalosis is also present. Diuretics are a saline-responsive cause of metabolic alkalosis, and liver disease with diuretics is the listed setting.

set1.topic: Metabolic acidosis: causes and the anion gap
set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
set1.q: A 55-year-old woman has received large volumes of normal saline for 3 days after abdominal surgery. She also takes acetaminophen for pain, has nasogastric suction, and takes a loop diuretic for edema. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.32 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 115 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which part of her care should be limited?
opts: Further large-volume normal saline

Correct. Low pH and bicarbonate make a metabolic acidosis, and the gap is 140 - (15 + 115) = 10, normal, with a high chloride. Saline infusion is a normal-gap cause, so the infusion feeding the acidosis is the part to limit.
Her acetaminophen for pain
Acetaminophen toxicity causes a raised-gap acidosis through 5-oxoproline. Her gap is 10, normal. Tell: a normal gap with a high chloride fits saline, not acetaminophen.
competing diagnosis
Her nasogastric suction
Gastric suction removes acid and causes a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis. Her pH is 7.32 with a low bicarbonate. Tell: suction pushes the pH up, so it is not feeding this acidosis.
reversed direction or value
Her loop diuretic for edema
Diuretics cause a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis with a high bicarbonate. Her bicarbonate is 15. Tell: a diuretic raises the bicarbonate; hers has fallen.
reversed direction or value

set1.q: A 33-year-old woman with self-induced vomiting has a metabolic alkalosis. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.51 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 47 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 36 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Her potassium is 2.9 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L). Her vomiting has stopped and saline has been started. Which approach to her potassium should be avoided?
opts: Replacing well beyond the measured deficit

Correct. Much of the low potassium in alkalosis is a shift into cells. Potassium deficits are treated if needed, but overcorrection is to be avoided, because as the alkalosis corrects potassium shifts back out of the cells.
Replacing potassium alongside her fluids
Treating fluid and potassium deficits is part of treating saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, and her potassium of 2.9 is low. Tell: replacement is right; overshooting is the danger.
reversed direction or value
Rechecking potassium as the alkalosis corrects
Rechecking is how overcorrection is avoided, since potassium moves back out of cells as the pH falls. Tell: monitoring is the safe practice, not the one to avoid.
reversed direction or value
Treating the cause of her vomiting
Treating the underlying condition is the first step for metabolic alkalosis. Tell: the item to avoid is excess potassium, not care of the cause.
reversed direction or value

set1.topic: Identifying the disorder step by step
set1.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
set1.q: A 58-year-old man is brought in confused with a low blood pressure, and the cause of his critical illness is not yet clear. Which initial testing best characterizes his acid-base status?
opts: Urine chloride before any blood testing
Urine chloride is used when a metabolic alkalosis has an unclear cause, after the blood gas has named the disorder. Tell: the blood gas and electrolytes come first.
wrong stage or severity
Arterial gas and electrolytes drawn together

Correct. The first step is to obtain an arterial blood gas and electrolytes simultaneously, so the bicarbonate on each can be compared to verify accuracy and the anion gap can be calculated. In a critically ill patient the acid-base type can assist the diagnosis.
Arterial gas now, electrolytes the next day
Drawing them a day apart loses the comparison of the two bicarbonate values and makes the anion gap unreliable. Tell: the gas and electrolytes are drawn at the same time.
wrong stage or severity
Electrolytes alone, adding a gas if abnormal
The anion gap can be abnormal even when sodium, chloride and bicarbonate are normal, and electrolytes alone give no pH or carbon dioxide. Tell: the disorder cannot be named without the gas.
wrong stage or severity

set1.io: Compare and contrast compensatory mechanisms for simple and mixed acid-base disorders.
set1.q: A 72-year-old woman has chronic respiratory acidosis from long-standing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.33 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 68 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 35 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). A student predicts her kidneys will bring her pH back to 7.40 with time. Which statement about her compensation is accurate?
opts: It moves pH toward normal without fully correcting it

Correct. Compensation will not fully correct the pH disturbance; the underlying condition must be corrected to restore balance. Her kidneys have raised the bicarbonate to 35, which pulls the pH up toward normal, but it remains 7.33.
It fully restores pH once 48 hours have passed

The chronic renal response is in place after 24 to 48 hours, but it still falls short of a normal pH; her pH is 7.33 despite years of disease. Tell: compensation narrows the gap to normal but does not close it.
reversed direction or value
It works through the lungs blowing off carbon dioxide

Lungs blowing off carbon dioxide compensate a metabolic acidosis. Her primary problem is respiratory, so the kidneys compensate by retaining bicarbonate. Tell: the compensating system is the other one.
confused mechanism or drug class
It overshoots, leaving her slightly alkalemic

Compensation does not overshoot into the opposite state; an alkalemic pH in a retainer would point to an added disorder. Her pH is 7.33. Tell: a simple disorder keeps the pH on the side of its primary problem.
reversed direction or value
set1.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 23, 34

set1.io: Compare and contrast compensatory mechanisms for simple and mixed acid-base disorders.
set1.q: A 67-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has had nasogastric suction for 3 days after bowel surgery. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.41 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 60 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 37 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). From a baseline carbon dioxide of 40 mm Hg and bicarbonate of 25 mEq/L, in chronic respiratory acidosis bicarbonate rises 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide. What does his bicarbonate indicate?
opts: A concurrent metabolic alkalosis

Correct. Chronic compensation predicts bicarbonate = 25 + 3.5 x (60 - 40) / 10 = 25 + 7 = 32. His is 37, 5 above prediction, so something beyond the kidneys is adding bicarbonate: loss of gastric acid by suction. A normal pH with a high carbon dioxide also signals a mixed disorder.
Appropriate chronic compensation

Appropriate chronic compensation would give a bicarbonate near 32, and compensation alone never returns the pH to a normal 7.41. His 37 overshoots. Tell: a bicarbonate above the chronic prediction adds a metabolic alkalosis.
wrong stage or severity
Appropriate acute compensation

Acute compensation adds only 1 per 10 mm Hg, predicting 25 + 2 = 27, far below his 37, and his lung disease is long-standing. Tell: the acute ratio fits a sudden rise over hours; it cannot explain a bicarbonate of 37.
wrong stage or severity
A concurrent metabolic acidosis

A concurrent metabolic acidosis would hold bicarbonate below the predicted 32. His is 37, above it. Tell: bicarbonate above prediction means metabolic alkalosis; below prediction means metabolic acidosis.
reversed direction or value

set1.q: A 58-year-old woman on dialysis for kidney failure missed a week of sessions, has vomited for 4 days and feels anxious. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.40 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 38 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 23 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 137 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 93 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Using 10 as the normal anion gap and 25 mEq/L as the normal bicarbonate, which part of her history best explains the metabolic alkalosis?
opts: Diarrhea from her illness
Diarrhea loses bicarbonate and gives a normal-gap acidosis with a high chloride; her chloride is 93, low. Tell: lower gastrointestinal losses drop bicarbonate; upper losses from vomiting raise it.
reversed direction or value
Her anxiety

Anxiety causes hyperventilation and a respiratory alkalosis, which lowers carbon dioxide; it does not raise bicarbonate, and her carbon dioxide of 38 is near normal. Tell: a change in gap larger than the change in bicarbonate needs a metabolic, alkalinizing cause such as vomiting.
confused mechanism or drug class
Her vomiting

Correct. Gap = 137 - (93 + 23) = 21, change in gap = 11, but change in bicarbonate = 25 - 23 = 2: a metabolic alkalosis is holding the bicarbonate up. Vomiting loses gastric hydrochloric acid, a saline-responsive cause, and her low chloride fits.
Her kidney failure

Kidney failure with uremia explains the raised gap of 21, the metabolic acidosis half of this pair. Tell: the alkalosis needs a cause that adds bicarbonate or removes acid, and vomiting removes gastric acid.
adjacent fact
set1.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 30, 50, 53

set1.io: Explain how acid-base disorders affect electrolytes and oxygenation.
set1.q: A 31-year-old woman has been breathing rapidly for 30 minutes during a panic attack. She has not vomited, has no diarrhea and takes no medicines. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.54 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 28 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 23 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Her potassium is 3.3 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L). Which process best accounts for her potassium level?
opts: Potassium lost through the gut from vomiting

Vomiting causes a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis with a high bicarbonate. She has not vomited, and her bicarbonate is 23 with a low carbon dioxide, a respiratory picture. Tell: the stem rules out vomiting.
ruled out by a stated finding
Severe depletion of total body potassium

Severe potassium depletion is a saline-unresponsive cause of metabolic alkalosis, with a high bicarbonate. Her bicarbonate is 23 and her low carbon dioxide drives the pH, and nothing in her history removes potassium from the body. Tell: her potassium has moved, not been lost.
adjacent fact
Potassium shifted into cells as hydrogen ions left them

Correct. A pH of 7.54 with a carbon dioxide of 28 is a respiratory alkalosis from anxiety. In alkalosis hydrogen ions shift out of cells and potassium shifts into cells, resulting in hypokalemia, with no potassium actually lost from the body.
Potassium shifted out of cells as hydrogen ions entered
That is the shift of acidosis, and it raises the serum potassium. Her pH is 7.54, alkalemic, so potassium moves the other way. Tell: a low potassium with a high pH is the alkalosis shift into cells.
reversed direction or value
set1.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 5, 39

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with chronic respiratory acidosis from kyphoscoliosis is intubated, and the ventilator lowers her carbon dioxide from 70 to 40 mm Hg within an hour. Her bicarbonate is 35 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which complication is she now at risk for?
opts: Cardiac arrhythmias and seizures

Correct. In chronic respiratory acidosis the kidneys have raised bicarbonate over days, and it falls slowly. Lowering carbon dioxide rapidly leaves that bicarbonate unopposed, and the alkalosis may cause cardiac arrhythmias, reduced cerebral perfusion and seizures.
Hyperkalemia from potassium leaving cells

Potassium leaves cells in acidosis. A rapid fall in her carbon dioxide with a bicarbonate of 35 creates an alkalosis, which moves potassium into cells and lowers it. Tell: the risk after over-correction is alkalosis, so think low potassium.
reversed direction or value
Improved oxygen delivery to tissues
Alkalosis increases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen and decreases delivery to tissues. Her sudden alkalosis worsens delivery. Tell: alkalosis holds oxygen on hemoglobin.
reversed direction or value
A worsening metabolic acidosis

Her retained bicarbonate of 35 is unopposed once the carbon dioxide falls, which produces alkalosis, not acidosis; a high bicarbonate after high carbon dioxide is the post-hypercapnia pattern. Tell: the leftover bicarbonate makes her alkalotic.
reversed direction or value
set1.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 34, 37, 5

set1.topic: Metabolic acidosis: Winter formula and the change in anion gap
set1.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
set1.q: A 41-year-old man has 4 days of diarrhea and has not eaten for a week; his serum albumin 4.6 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.25 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 21 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 9 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 137 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 110 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). His bicarbonate has fallen 16 while his anion gap has risen only 8. Which value should be examined next?
opts: The change in chloride

Correct. Gap = 137 - (110 + 9) = 18, change in gap 8; change in bicarbonate 25 - 9 = 16. When the bicarbonate falls more than the gap rises, check the change in chloride; if gap change plus chloride change accounts for the bicarbonate change, a normal-gap acidosis (diarrhea) joins the raised-gap one (starvation ketoacidosis).
The urine chloride

Urine chloride sorts metabolic alkalosis into saline-responsive and saline-unresponsive types. He has an acidosis, and the gap is too small for his bicarbonate fall. Tell: serum chloride change explains a bicarbonate fall larger than the gap rise.
adjacent fact
The albumin-corrected gap
His albumin of 4.6 is normal, so no correction is needed; the gap of 18 stands. Tell: the gap is corrected when albumin is low.
ruled out by a stated finding
The Winter formula prediction

Expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 9 + 8 = 21.5, range 19.5 to 23.5, and his 21 fits, so compensation is appropriate. It does not explain the metabolic mismatch. Tell: the mismatch between bicarbonate and gap is resolved by chloride.
confused mechanism or drug class

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
set1.q: A 26-year-old woman has episodes of rapid breathing and palpitations when she is anxious; her examination is otherwise normal. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 32 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 23 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Faster breathing will help clear the episodes
Faster breathing blows off more carbon dioxide and raises the pH further. Her carbon dioxide is already 32 from hyperventilation. Tell: the fix for over-breathing is slower breathing.
reversed direction or value
Daily potassium supplements prevent the episodes

Alkalosis can lower potassium by shifting it into cells, but supplements do not stop hyperventilation, and her episodes come from anxiety. Tell: treat the cause of the breathing, not a shifted electrolyte.
adjacent fact
She will need mechanical ventilation if they recur

Mechanical ventilation is for failing ventilation, as in severe respiratory acidosis. Her pH of 7.48 is a mild alkalosis that usually needs no treatment. Tell: mild anxiety hyperventilation is managed with breathing, not a ventilator.
wrong stage or severity
Slow, mindful breathing can ease the episodes

Correct. A pH of 7.48 with a low carbon dioxide is a mild respiratory alkalosis from anxiety. With a pH below 7.50 treatment is usually not required; treating the anxiety and mindful breathing to control the hyperventilation are the measures.
set1.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 39, 40

set1.q: A 63-year-old woman with cirrhosis has an infection and low blood pressure; her serum albumin 1.9 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 31 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 133 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 105 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Her gap is 12 and her carbon dioxide fits the predicted compensation. Which step should come next?
opts: Compare changes in gap and bicarbonate

That comparison detects a hidden metabolic alkalosis only when the gap is high, and her gap has not yet been corrected. Using an uncorrected 12 would mislead. Tell: correct the gap first, then compare the changes.
wrong stage or severity
Repeat the Winter formula
Her carbon dioxide already fits the predicted range (1.5 x 16 + 8 = 32, range 30 to 34), so compensation is settled. Tell: the open question is the gap, and with albumin 1.9 it must be corrected.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct the anion gap for albumin

Correct. Her gap = 133 - (105 + 16) = 12 looks normal, but albumin 1.9 is 2.6 below 4.5, so the corrected gap = 12 + 2.5 x 2.6 = 18.5, raised. The gap must be corrected when albumin is abnormal, and doing so changes her diagnosis to a raised-gap acidosis.
Measure the urine chloride

Urine chloride separates saline-responsive from saline-unresponsive metabolic alkalosis. She has an acidosis (pH 7.34, bicarbonate 16). Tell: for an acidosis with low albumin, the next number to fix is the gap.
adjacent fact
set1.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 8, 57, 48

set1.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
set1.q: A 44-year-old woman took a large overdose of aspirin (a salicylate) 6 hours ago and is breathing rapidly. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 25 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 18 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 96 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorders are present?
opts: Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation

Renal compensation lowers bicarbonate, but it does not create unmeasured anions: compensation for a respiratory disorder never gives a large gap, and hers is 140 - (96 + 18) = 26. Tell: a gap above 20 means a primary metabolic disorder.
wrong stage or severity
Respiratory alkalosis with respiratory acidosis

Only one respiratory disorder can exist at a time; a patient cannot breathe too fast and too slow at once. Multiple metabolic disorders can coexist with one respiratory one. Tell: a second disorder alongside a respiratory one must be metabolic.
confused mechanism or drug class
Raised-gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation

Compensation never overshoots: a primary metabolic acidosis with compensation keeps the pH below 7.35. Her pH is 7.48, alkalemic, so a respiratory alkalosis is driving it. Tell: an alkalemic pH with a raised gap means two primary processes.
reversed direction or value
Respiratory alkalosis with raised-gap metabolic acidosis

Correct. The pH of 7.48 with a carbon dioxide of 25 is a respiratory alkalosis. But the gap = 140 - (96 + 18) = 26, above 20, and a large gap is never produced by a respiratory disorder alone, so a raised-gap metabolic acidosis is also present. Salicylates are a listed cause of both.
set1.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 26, 23, 44, 40

set1.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
set1.q: A 31-year-old woman has been treated for diabetic ketoacidosis with saline and insulin for 10 hours; her ketones are clearing. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.28 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 24 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 11 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 141 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 112 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Using 10 as the normal anion gap and 25 mEq/L as the normal bicarbonate, which acid-base disorders are present?
opts: Raised-gap metabolic acidosis alone

Ketoacidosis alone would give a change in gap about equal to the change in bicarbonate. Hers are 8 and 14, with a high chloride. Tell: a bicarbonate fall larger than the gap rise, plus high chloride, means a second, normal-gap acidosis.
wrong stage or severity
Raised-gap metabolic acidosis with metabolic alkalosis

A concurrent metabolic alkalosis would make the change in gap bigger than the change in bicarbonate. Hers is smaller, 8 against 14. Tell: gap change exceeding bicarbonate change means alkalosis; the reverse means check the chloride.
reversed direction or value
Metabolic acidosis with respiratory acidosis

Expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 11 + 8 = 24.5, range 22.5 to 26.5, and hers is 24, inside it, so the respiratory compensation is appropriate. Tell: work the Winter formula before adding a respiratory disorder.
ruled out by a stated finding
Raised-gap with normal-gap metabolic acidosis

Correct. Gap = 141 - (112 + 11) = 18, change in gap = 8; change in bicarbonate = 25 - 11 = 14. The bicarbonate fell more than the gap rose, and her chloride of 112 is high, so a normal-gap acidosis has joined the clearing ketoacidosis, the pattern listed for treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis.

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman in septic shock from pneumonia was given an opioid and a benzodiazepine for agitation and is now drowsy. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.21 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 41 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 137 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 99 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Give oxygen and recheck in a day
Oxygen does not remove a respiratory depressant or reverse septic shock, and waiting leaves both causes untreated with a pH of 7.21. Tell: the rule is to find and treat each underlying condition.
wrong stage or severity
Increase sedation to calm her breathing

More sedation deepens the respiratory acidosis: her carbon dioxide is already above prediction. Tell: respiratory depressants such as narcotics and benzodiazepines are stopped, not increased, in respiratory acidosis.
reversed direction or value
Stop the sedatives and treat the sepsis

Correct. Gap = 137 - (99 + 16) = 22, a raised-gap lactic acidosis; expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 16 + 8 = 32, range 30 to 34, and her 41 is above it, a concurrent respiratory acidosis. Both causes must be found and treated: stop the respiratory depressants and treat the infection.
Treat the sepsis and continue sedatives

Treating sepsis addresses the lactic acidosis, but her carbon dioxide of 41 is above the predicted 30 to 34; the opioid and benzodiazepine are suppressing her breathing. Tell: in a mixed disorder, treat both causes.
wrong stage or severity
set1.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 36, 28, 49, 63

set1.q: A 41-year-old woman has bipolar disorder treated with lithium and type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Routine testing shows sodium 136 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 106 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 26 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L), albumin 4.4 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL), and no monoclonal protein. Which part of her history best accounts for her anion gap?
opts: A plasma cell dyscrasia
A plasma cell dyscrasia lowers the gap through a cationic monoclonal protein. Her testing shows no monoclonal protein. Tell: the stem removes this cause and leaves her lithium.
ruled out by a stated finding
Lithium

Correct. Her gap is 136 - (26 + 106) = 4, below the normal 6 to 12. A decreased gap comes from added abnormal cations such as lithium, which are not counted in the formula. Her normal albumin and absent monoclonal protein remove the other low-gap causes.
Metformin
Metformin is a cause of raised-gap metabolic acidosis, which would push the gap above 12 and lower the bicarbonate. Her gap is 4 and her bicarbonate 26. Tell: metformin raises the gap; hers is low.
reversed direction or value
A low serum albumin
A low albumin is the usual reason for a low gap, but her albumin is 4.4 g/dL, normal, so there is nothing to correct for. Tell: check the albumin first; when it is normal, look for an added cation.
ruled out by a stated finding
set1.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 7, 48

set1.q: A 74-year-old woman is drowsy 2 days after hip surgery. She takes an opioid for pain, a benzodiazepine at night for anxiety, a thiazide for hypertension and an inhaled bronchodilator for asthma. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.26 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 62 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 27 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which of her medicines should be stopped?
opts: The thiazide diuretic alone

Diuretics cause a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis with a raised bicarbonate. Her problem is a high carbon dioxide from reduced breathing. Tell: look for respiratory depressants on the list, not diuretics.
adjacent fact
The opioid and the benzodiazepine

Correct. Low pH with a high carbon dioxide and a bicarbonate only slightly raised is an acute respiratory acidosis. Treatment starts with the cause and a medicine review: stop respiratory depressants, narcotics and benzodiazepines, which reduce ventilation.
The thiazide and the bronchodilator

A thiazide causes metabolic alkalosis, not a respiratory acidosis, and a bronchodilator opens the airways rather than depressing breathing. Tell: the drugs to stop in respiratory acidosis are the respiratory depressants.
adjacent fact
The inhaled bronchodilator alone

Her bronchodilator treats bronchospasm, itself a cause of respiratory acidosis, so stopping it could worsen ventilation. Tell: the sedating drugs, not the airway drug, explain a drowsy patient with a high carbon dioxide.
reversed direction or value
set1.cite: PAJ5510 Acid Base Disorders II MBF2026sc.pptx, Slides 32, 36

set1.q: A 74-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease takes a diuretic for leg swelling. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.42 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 64 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 40 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 139 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 89 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). From a baseline carbon dioxide of 40 mm Hg and bicarbonate of 25 mEq/L, in chronic respiratory acidosis bicarbonate rises 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide, and in metabolic alkalosis carbon dioxide rises 0.75 mm Hg per 1 mEq/L rise in bicarbonate. Which acid-base disorders are present?
opts: Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic alkalosis

Correct. Chronic compensation predicts bicarbonate = 25 + 3.5 x 2.4 = about 33; hers is 40, higher. Read from the metabolic side, expected carbon dioxide = 40 + 0.75 x 15 = about 51; hers is 64, higher. Both disorders are present and the pH sits at a normal 7.42, the listed pattern for this disease on diuretics.
Chronic respiratory acidosis with appropriate compensation

Appropriate chronic compensation would bring bicarbonate to about 25 + 3.5 x 2.4 = 33, and her 40 is well past it. Compensation also never returns the pH fully to normal. Tell: a normal pH with a high carbon dioxide and a high bicarbonate is two disorders.
wrong stage or severity
Metabolic alkalosis with appropriate compensation

Respiratory compensation for a bicarbonate of 40 predicts carbon dioxide = 40 + 0.75 x 15 = about 51. Hers is 64, too high for compensation alone, which fits her lung disease. Tell: a carbon dioxide above prediction means a concurrent respiratory acidosis.
wrong stage or severity
Acute respiratory acidosis with metabolic alkalosis

An acute respiratory acidosis raises bicarbonate only 1 per 10 mm Hg, and her chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has had far longer than 24 to 48 hours. The respiratory side here is chronic. Tell: a long-standing lung disease gives the chronic 3.5 ratio.
wrong stage or severity

set1.topic: Metabolic acidosis: Winter formula and the change in anion gap
set1.io: Compare and contrast compensatory mechanisms for simple and mixed acid-base disorders.
set1.q: A 49-year-old man with alcoholic ketoacidosis has vomited repeatedly for 2 days. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.36 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 33 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 18 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 136 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 90 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Using 10 as the normal anion gap and 25 mEq/L as the normal bicarbonate, what does comparing the change in anion gap with the change in bicarbonate show?
opts: A raised-gap acidosis alone
Ketoacidosis alone would drop bicarbonate by about the gap's rise, to near 25 - 18 = 7. His is 18. Tell: a change in gap far larger than the change in bicarbonate means an added metabolic alkalosis.
wrong stage or severity
An added normal-gap acidosis

An added normal-gap acidosis makes bicarbonate fall more than the gap rises, with a high chloride. His bicarbonate fell less (7 against 18) and his chloride of 90 is low. Tell: vomiting lowers chloride; a normal-gap acidosis raises it.
reversed direction or value
An added respiratory alkalosis

The change comparison detects metabolic processes, and respiratory ones are judged with the Winter formula: 1.5 x 18 + 8 = 35, range 33 to 37, which his 33 meets. Tell: gap change exceeding bicarbonate change is a metabolic alkalosis.
confused mechanism or drug class
An added metabolic alkalosis

Correct. Gap = 136 - (90 + 18) = 28, change in gap = 18; change in bicarbonate = 25 - 18 = 7. The gap rose far more than the bicarbonate fell, so a metabolic alkalosis from vomiting is holding bicarbonate up, detectable here because the gap is high.

set1.io: Explain mechanisms for maintaining acid-base homeostasis.
set1.q: A 37-year-old man has had profuse watery diarrhea for 4 days and is breathing deeply. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.32 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What does his carbon dioxide of 30 represent?
opts: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis

Correct. A low pH with a low bicarbonate is a metabolic acidosis, and diarrhea is a common cause. When the cause is metabolic, compensation is respiratory: increased breathing lowers carbon dioxide, which pulls the pH toward normal without fully correcting it.
A primary respiratory alkalosis

A primary respiratory alkalosis would raise the pH above 7.45. His pH is 7.32, acidemic, so the low carbon dioxide cannot be the primary problem. Tell: the pH points to the low bicarbonate as the primary change.
ruled out by a stated finding
Renal compensation for respiratory alkalosis
Renal compensation changes bicarbonate, not carbon dioxide, and it would follow a primary respiratory alkalosis with a high pH. His pH is 7.32. Tell: carbon dioxide changes are the lungs' work.
confused mechanism or drug class
Carbon dioxide retention from hypoventilation
Hypoventilation raises carbon dioxide above 45. His is 30, low, from breathing more. Tell: a low carbon dioxide means more ventilation, not less.
reversed direction or value

set1.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
set1.q: A 71-year-old man with severe pneumonia is confused and tiring, with shallow respirations and cool, mottled skin. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.20 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 40 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 141 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 105 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorders are present?
opts: Raised-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis

A concurrent respiratory alkalosis would push carbon dioxide below the predicted 28.5 to 32.5. His 40 is above it, and he is tiring with shallow breaths. Tell: a normal-looking carbon dioxide of 40 is too high for a bicarbonate of 15.
reversed direction or value
Raised-gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation

Appropriate compensation would bring carbon dioxide down to about 28.5 to 32.5 (1.5 x 15 + 8, plus or minus 2). His 40 has not fallen at all. Tell: a carbon dioxide inside its normal range can still be abnormal when the bicarbonate is low.
wrong stage or severity
Normal-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory acidosis

His gap is 141 - (105 + 15) = 21, well above 6 to 12, and his chloride of 105 is normal, so this is not the hyperchloremic normal-gap type. Tell: calculate the gap before naming the acidosis; poor perfusion gives a raised-gap lactic acidosis.
ruled out by a stated finding
Raised-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory acidosis

Correct. Gap = 141 - (105 + 15) = 21, raised. Expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 15 + 8 = 30.5, range about 28.5 to 32.5; his 40 is well above it, so he is not blowing off enough carbon dioxide, a concurrent respiratory acidosis. Severe pneumonia is a listed setting for this pair.

set1.q: A 70-year-old man with heart failure, poor tissue perfusion and a low albumin is admitted. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.32 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 32 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 108 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). His albumin is 2.9 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). What is his anion gap after correction for his albumin?
opts: This is the uncorrected gap, 140 - (16 + 108) = 16. With an albumin of 2.9 g/dL the gap must be corrected upward by 4. Tell: a low albumin makes the measured gap read too low.
wrong stage or severity
This counts the albumin drop from 3.5, the bottom of the normal range: (3.5 - 2.9) x 2.5 = 1.5. The correction counts from 4.5 g/dL, a 1.6 g/dL drop worth 4. Tell: start the correction at 4.5.
reversed direction or value

Correct. The measured gap is 140 - (16 + 108) = 16. His albumin is 4.5 - 2.9 = 1.6 g/dL below 4.5, and 1.6 x 2.5 = 4, so the corrected gap is 16 + 4 = 20, a raised gap that fits lactic acidosis from poor perfusion.
This counts the albumin drop from 5.5, the top of the normal range: (5.5 - 2.9) x 2.5 = 6.5. The correction counts from 4.5 g/dL, a 1.6 g/dL drop worth 4. Tell: start the correction at 4.5.

set1.q: A 64-year-old man has an ileal loop bladder (a ureteral diversion) after bladder cancer surgery, takes isoniazid for latent tuberculosis, and has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Serum ketones are negative. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 31 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 139 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 113 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 16 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which part of his history best accounts for this blood gas?
opts: Metformin
Metformin causes a raised-gap acidosis. His gap is 10 and his chloride 113. Tell: metformin raises the gap; his is normal.
competing diagnosis
Diabetic ketoacidosis, active
Active diabetic ketoacidosis is a raised-gap cause, and his ketones are negative with a gap of 10. Tell: ketoacids add unmeasured anions; his gap has not risen.
ruled out by a stated finding
The ileal loop bladder

Correct. Low pH and bicarbonate make a metabolic acidosis, and the gap is 139 - (16 + 113) = 10, normal, with a high chloride. Ureteral diversion and the ileal loop bladder are on the normal-gap list. Isoniazid and metformin raise the gap.
Isoniazid
Isoniazid is on the raised-gap list, with a gap above 12. His gap is 10. Tell: a normal gap with a high chloride rules out the raised-gap drugs.
competing diagnosis

set1.q: A 69-year-old woman with urosepsis in the intensive care unit is breathing 30 times a minute. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.41 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 21 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 13 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 142 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 103 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). What is her anion gap?
opts: This is the change in bicarbonate, 25 - 13 = 12, not the gap. The gap is 142 - (103 + 13) = 26. Tell: the gap needs sodium, chloride and bicarbonate together.
adjacent fact
This is the change in gap, 26 - 10 = 16, one step too far. The gap itself is 142 - (103 + 13) = 26. Tell: calculate the gap first, then subtract 10 only when comparing changes.
adjacent fact

Correct. Gap = sodium - (chloride + bicarbonate) = 142 - (103 + 13) = 142 - 116 = 26, well above 6 to 12. A raised-gap acidosis with a normal pH means a second process: her carbon dioxide of 21 is below the predicted 25.5 to 29.5, a concurrent respiratory alkalosis.
This is sodium minus chloride alone, 142 - 103, leaving out the bicarbonate. The gap subtracts both: 142 - (103 + 13) = 26. Tell: both measured anions, chloride and bicarbonate, come off the sodium.
adjacent fact

set1.q: A 59-year-old man with 5 days of diarrhea was given a benzodiazepine overnight for agitation and is now drowsy with slow, shallow breathing. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.21 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 36 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 139 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 115 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). opts: Raised-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory acidosis

Normal-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory acidosis

Correct. Gap = 139 - (115 + 14) = 10, normal, with a high chloride: the normal-gap acidosis of diarrhea. Expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29, range 27 to 31; his 36 is above it, a concurrent respiratory acidosis from the respiratory depressant.
Normal-gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation

Appropriate compensation would bring carbon dioxide down to 27 to 31. His is 36, too high, which fits slow, shallow breathing after a sedative. Tell: a carbon dioxide inside the normal 35 to 45 can still be too high for a low bicarbonate.
wrong stage or severity
Normal-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis
A concurrent respiratory alkalosis would push carbon dioxide below 27. His is 36, above the predicted range. Tell: above the Winter range is respiratory acidosis, below it is respiratory alkalosis.

set1.q: A 54-year-old man with chronic kidney failure has fatigue. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.29 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 103 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L), potassium 4.0 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L). What is his anion gap?
opts: This uses a normal bicarbonate of 24 in place of his measured 14: 138 - (24 + 103) = 11. The formula takes the measured value, which is 14. Tell: plug in the patient's own bicarbonate, not the normal one.
confused mechanism or drug class

Correct. Anion gap = sodium - (bicarbonate + chloride) = 138 - (14 + 103) = 138 - 117 = 21, above the normal 6 to 12. A raised gap with a low pH and low bicarbonate is a raised-gap metabolic acidosis, and renal failure is on that list.

This adds his potassium of 4.0 to the sodium: (138 + 4) - (14 + 103) = 25. The anion gap formula used here is sodium minus chloride and bicarbonate, with no potassium. Tell: potassium is not part of the calculation.

This subtracts only the chloride: 138 - 103 = 35, leaving out the bicarbonate. The gap subtracts both measured anions, chloride and bicarbonate. Tell: two anions come off the sodium, not one.

set1.q: A 39-year-old man has had nasogastric suction for 4 days after bowel surgery and has dry mucous membranes. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.50 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 48 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 36 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). His potassium is 3.0 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L), and his urine chloride is low. Along with stopping the suction, which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Fluid restriction with a diuretic
He is already volume depleted, and diuretics are themselves a cause of saline-responsive alkalosis. Tell: a low urine chloride with dry mucous membranes calls for fluid, not fluid removal.
reversed direction or value
A hydrocortisone infusion
Corticosteroids are a contributor to metabolic alkalosis and are among the drugs to stop, and hydrocortisone has more mineralocorticoid activity than prednisone. Tell: steroids worsen this alkalosis.
reversed direction or value
Ventilation to lower his carbon dioxide
His carbon dioxide of 48 is compensation for the alkalosis. Lowering it would raise the pH further. Tell: treat the metabolic cause, not the compensation.
wrong stage or severity
Saline with potassium replacement

Correct. Gastric suction causes a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, confirmed by the low urine chloride, and he is volume depleted. Treatment is to stop contributors such as suction and treat the fluid and potassium deficits.

set1.q: A 77-year-old woman takes a thiazide for hypertension and has had 3 days of weakness. Her blood pressure is 126/74 mm Hg. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.47 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 47 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 33 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Her potassium is 3.1 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L), and her urine chloride is low. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Add a loop diuretic to the thiazide therapy
Diuretics cause saline-responsive alkalosis, so adding a second one worsens both the alkalosis and the volume loss. Tell: discontinue the diuretic; do not add another.
reversed direction or value
Start hydrocortisone and continue the thiazide
Corticosteroids, particularly hydrocortisone, add mineralocorticoid effect and are among the contributors to stop, and the thiazide is the cause. Tell: both choices push the bicarbonate higher.
reversed direction or value
Restrict her salt and fluid intake for now
A low urine chloride marks the saline-responsive group, which is volume contracted. Restricting salt and fluid deepens that. Tell: saline-responsive means give fluid.
reversed direction or value
Stop the thiazide; give fluid and potassium

Correct. A pH of 7.47 with a bicarbonate of 33 and a low urine chloride is a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, and diuretics are a cause. Treatment stops the contributor and treats the fluid and potassium deficits, without overcorrecting.

set1.q: A 72-year-old man has chronic kidney failure that has worsened over months, adrenal insufficiency on hormone replacement, glaucoma treated with an oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, and leg edema treated with a loop diuretic. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.32 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 103 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which part of his history best accounts for this blood gas?
opts: The loop diuretic
Diuretics cause a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis with a high bicarbonate. His bicarbonate is 15 and his pH 7.32. Tell: a diuretic pushes the pH the other way.
reversed direction or value
His kidney failure

Correct. Low pH and bicarbonate make a metabolic acidosis, and the gap is 138 - (15 + 103) = 20, above 12. Renal failure, acute or chronic, is one of the big four raised-gap causes. His other conditions do not raise the gap.
His adrenal insufficiency
Adrenal insufficiency causes a normal-gap acidosis, with a gap of 6 to 12 and a high chloride. His gap is 20 and his chloride 103. Tell: adrenal insufficiency is on the normal-gap list.
competing diagnosis
The carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors cause a normal-gap acidosis by bicarbonate loss. His gap is 20. Tell: a raised gap needs unmeasured anions, which failing kidneys retain.
competing diagnosis

set1.q: A 67-year-old man with severe pneumonia is increasingly somnolent. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.16 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 88 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 30 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). His partial pressure of oxygen is 36 mm Hg (normal 80 to 100 mm Hg). Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Repeat the blood gas in 24 hours

Waiting suits a stable patient, not one whose carbon dioxide is above 80 with an oxygen below 40. These values mark an acute, severe impairment that needs ventilation now. Tell: the thresholds call for action, not observation.
wrong stage or severity
Secure the airway and ventilate mechanically

Correct. A carbon dioxide above 80 mm Hg with life-threatening hypoxia (partial pressure of oxygen below 40) is an acute, severe failure of carbon dioxide excretion. He needs adequate ventilation, which may mean an emergency airway and a mechanical ventilator, plus oxygen.
Withhold oxygen to protect his breathing drive

Oxygen is part of treatment, and his partial pressure of oxygen of 36 is life-threatening. Careful oxygen applies to chronic retainers, and even then it is given, not withheld. Tell: severe hypoxia is treated, not tolerated.
reversed direction or value
Coach him in slow, mindful breathing

Mindful breathing helps control the hyperventilation of respiratory alkalosis. He is under-ventilating with a carbon dioxide of 88 and is somnolent. Tell: breathing coaching is for too much breathing, not too little.
adjacent fact

set2.q: A 61-year-old woman takes hydrocortisone for a chronic inflammatory condition and must stay on a corticosteroid. She has a metabolic alkalosis. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.49 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 47 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 34 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which change to her corticosteroid is most appropriate?
opts: Keep hydrocortisone at the same dose
Hydrocortisone has more mineralocorticoid activity, which drives the alkalosis, so leaving it unchanged keeps the contributor in place. Tell: change the steroid or lower the dose.
wrong stage or severity
Switch to cortisone
Cortisone sits with hydrocortisone on the side to move away from, with more mineralocorticoid activity. Tell: the preferred agents are prednisone and methylprednisolone.
adjacent fact
Raise the hydrocortisone dose
A higher dose adds mineralocorticoid effect and worsens the alkalosis; the advice is to decrease the dose if possible. Tell: dose goes down, not up.
reversed direction or value
Switch to prednisone

Correct. If a patient with metabolic alkalosis requires corticosteroids, lower the dose or change to one with less mineralocorticoid activity: prednisone or methylprednisolone rather than cortisone or hydrocortisone.

set2.io: Explain mechanisms for maintaining acid-base homeostasis.
set2.q: A 68-year-old man has had obesity hypoventilation syndrome for many years. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.33 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 66 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 34 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). For respiratory acidosis, bicarbonate is expected to rise 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide when acute and 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg when chronic, from baselines of 40 mm Hg and 25 mEq/L. Which process accounts for his bicarbonate of 34?
opts: The kidneys retaining bicarbonate over days

Correct. A primary respiratory acidosis is compensated by the kidneys, which retain bicarbonate over hours to days. A chronic rise of 26 mm Hg predicts 25 + 3.5 x 2.6 = about 34, exactly his value, so this is the expected renal compensation.
The lungs retaining carbon dioxide to compensate

Lungs adjusting carbon dioxide is the compensation for a metabolic disorder. His carbon dioxide of 66 is the primary problem, so the compensation must come from the other system. Tell: respiratory cause, renal compensation.
confused mechanism or drug class
A second, primary metabolic alkalosis

An added metabolic alkalosis would push the bicarbonate above the predicted value. The chronic rule predicts about 34, and his is 34. Tell: a bicarbonate that matches the expected compensation needs no second disorder.
competing diagnosis
The kidneys excreting acid within minutes

Renal control of bicarbonate occurs over hours to days, not minutes; the lungs are the fast system. His history spans years, which is why the larger chronic rise is seen. Tell: kidneys are slow, lungs are quick.
wrong stage or severity

set2.q: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis and a low albumin has had watery diarrhea for 6 days. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 36 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 136 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 112 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). His albumin is 2.5 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). His anion gap calculates to 5. Which step comes next in interpreting the gap?
opts: Screen for a plasma cell dyscrasia

Plasma cell dyscrasias lower the gap through cationic paraproteins, but they are considered only when the gap stays low after correction. His corrected gap is 10, normal. Tell: rule out the low albumin first.
wrong stage or severity
Check for bromide intoxication

Bromide intoxication is another rare cause of a low gap, kept for a gap that remains low once albumin is accounted for. His albumin is 2.5 g/dL and explains the low value. Tell: the common reason for a low gap is the albumin.
wrong stage or severity
Search the raised-gap causes

The raised-gap list is used when the gap is above 12. His measured gap is 5 and his corrected gap 10, both at or below normal, so the normal-gap list applies, and diarrhea is on it. Tell: correct first, then pick the list.
reversed direction or value
Correct the gap for his low albumin

Correct. A low gap is most often a low albumin, and the gap must be corrected when albumin is abnormal. Adding 2.5 for each 1 g/dL below 4.5 gives 5 + 5 = 10, a normal gap, which fits a normal-gap metabolic acidosis from his diarrhea.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
set2.q: A 68-year-old man with uremia from kidney failure has vomited for 5 days and is dry on examination. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.41 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 41 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 25 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 143 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 97 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Using 10 as the normal anion gap and 25 mEq/L as the normal bicarbonate, which treatment approach is most appropriate?
opts: Replace fluids and treat the kidney failure

Correct. Gap = 143 - (97 + 25) = 21, change in gap = 11, change in bicarbonate = 0: a uremic acidosis with a metabolic alkalosis from vomiting. Both causes need treatment: replace his fluid deficit for the vomiting and treat the uremia.
Give bicarbonate to treat the acidosis

His bicarbonate is 25 and his pH 7.41; adding alkali would worsen the metabolic alkalosis, and alkali ingestion is itself a listed alkalosis cause. Tell: the normal bicarbonate reflects two opposing processes, so treat the causes.
wrong stage or severity
No treatment since his pH is normal

A normal pH hides two disorders here: the raised gap of 21 and a metabolic alkalosis from vomiting. Compensation will not fully correct the pH, so normal values with a raised gap mean a mixed disorder. Tell: always calculate the gap.

Treat the vomiting alone

set2.q: A 45-year-old man has renal tubular acidosis, irritable bowel syndrome with intermittent diarrhea, and glaucoma treated with an oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. His roommate found him confused beside an open container of antifreeze. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.23 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 22 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 9 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 105 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 9 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which part of his history best accounts for this blood gas?
opts: The carbonic anhydrase inhibitor
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors cause a normal-gap acidosis by loss of bicarbonate. His gap of 26 needs a raised-gap cause. Tell: this drug is on the normal-gap list, not the toxin list.
competing diagnosis
Ethylene glycol in the antifreeze

Correct. Low pH with a bicarbonate of 9 is a metabolic acidosis, and the gap is 140 - (9 + 105) = 26, well above 12. Ethylene glycol is a toxic alcohol on the raised-gap list. His other conditions all cause a normal-gap acidosis.
Renal tubular acidosis

Renal tubular acidosis causes a normal-gap acidosis through chloride retention, with a gap of 6 to 12 and a high chloride. His gap is 26 and his chloride 105. Tell: calculate the gap before choosing a list.
competing diagnosis
Intermittent diarrhea
Diarrhea causes a normal-gap acidosis by gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss, with a high chloride. His gap is 26. Tell: bicarbonate loss leaves the gap normal; a toxin adds unmeasured anions.
competing diagnosis

set2.q: A 46-year-old woman has weakness. Her blood pressure is normal, and she reports no vomiting and no medicines. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 47 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 34 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). The cause of her disorder is unclear. Which test best narrows the list of causes?
opts: Serum anion gap
The anion gap sorts the causes of metabolic acidosis into raised-gap and normal-gap lists. Her pH is 7.48, an alkalosis. Tell: alkalosis is sorted by urine chloride.
adjacent fact
Serum albumin
Albumin is used to correct the anion gap in acidosis. It does not separate the causes of metabolic alkalosis. Tell: albumin adjusts the gap; urine chloride sorts alkalosis.
adjacent fact
Urine bicarbonate

Metabolic alkalosis is sorted by urine chloride, not urine bicarbonate, so urine bicarbonate is not the test that splits the causes of alkalosis. Tell: the sorting test is urine chloride, which is low or high.
confused mechanism or drug class
Urine chloride

Correct. A pH of 7.48 with a bicarbonate of 34 is a metabolic alkalosis. When its cause is unclear, measuring urine chloride separates the saline-responsive causes (low urine chloride) from the saline-unresponsive causes (high urine chloride).

set2.topic: Normal values and the anion gap
set2.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
set2.q: A 76-year-old woman with long-standing poor nutrition becomes confused with a low blood pressure and cool extremities. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 36 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 137 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 106 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Her albumin is 2.1 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). Which acid-base disorder do her results show?
opts: Raised anion gap metabolic acidosis

Correct. Low pH and low bicarbonate make a metabolic acidosis. The measured gap is 137 - (19 + 106) = 12, but her albumin is 2.4 g/dL below 4.5, adding 2.4 x 2.5 = 6, so the corrected gap is 18, above 12. Poor perfusion causes lactic acidosis, a raised-gap cause.
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
This reads the uncorrected gap of 12 as normal. With an albumin of 2.1 g/dL the gap must be corrected, and it rises to 18. Tell: a low albumin can hide a raised gap inside the normal range.
wrong stage or severity
Respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
Respiratory acidosis needs a carbon dioxide above 45 with a raised bicarbonate. Hers is 36 with a bicarbonate of 19. Tell: the low bicarbonate, not the carbon dioxide, explains her low pH.
ruled out by a stated finding
Respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
Respiratory alkalosis has a pH above 7.45 with a low carbon dioxide. Her pH is 7.34, acidemic. Tell: compensation never pushes the pH past normal, so an acidemic pH rules out a primary alkalosis.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.topic: Identifying the disorder step by step
set2.io: Identify simple and mixed acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
set2.q: A 49-year-old woman is evaluated for fatigue. Her arterial blood gas shows pH 7.40 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 40 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 24 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). A serum panel drawn at the same moment shows a bicarbonate of 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Use the panel bicarbonate and proceed
A bicarbonate of 14 with a pH of 7.40 and a carbon dioxide of 40 does not fit, and taking it on trust skips the accuracy check. Tell: verify first when the two values disagree.
wrong stage or severity
Average the two values and proceed
An average of an accurate and an inaccurate value is still inaccurate. The comparison exists to catch a bad result. Tell: disagreeing values are rechecked, not blended.
common lay belief
Recheck both, as the bicarbonates disagree

Correct. The bicarbonate on the blood gas and on the electrolytes is compared to verify accuracy before any further step. A difference of 10 mEq/L between samples drawn together means one result is unreliable, so neither can carry the analysis yet.
Use the gas bicarbonate and proceed
Choosing one value skips the accuracy check, and the analysis could rest on the wrong number. Tell: two simultaneous bicarbonates that disagree are a warning to verify, not a choice to make.
wrong stage or severity

set2.q: A 70-year-old man with long-standing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and chronic carbon dioxide retention has an exacerbation. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.32 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 74 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 37 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). His partial pressure of oxygen is 52 mm Hg (normal 80 to 100 mm Hg). Which approach should be avoided?
opts: Driving his carbon dioxide down rapidly

Correct. His bicarbonate of 37 shows chronic renal compensation. Treatment is similar to acute disease but with careful oxygen, because a rapidly falling carbon dioxide in chronic respiratory acidosis may trigger the complications of alkalosis: cardiac arrhythmias, reduced cerebral perfusion and seizures.
Treating the cause of the exacerbation

Treating the underlying condition is the first step of respiratory acidosis treatment, acute or chronic. Tell: the risk in a chronic retainer comes from correcting carbon dioxide too fast, not from treating its cause.
reversed direction or value
Giving oxygen in carefully titrated amounts
Careful oxygen administration is exactly what chronic respiratory acidosis calls for, and his partial pressure of oxygen of 52 is low. Tell: oxygen is given with care, not avoided.
reversed direction or value
Reviewing his medicines for sedatives

Looking at the medication list and stopping respiratory depressants is part of treatment in both acute and chronic respiratory acidosis. Tell: a medicine review helps; a rapid fall in carbon dioxide harms.
reversed direction or value

set2.topic: Metabolic acidosis: causes and the anion gap
set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
set2.q: A 59-year-old woman has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, takes aspirin daily, takes isoniazid for latent tuberculosis, and has had profuse watery diarrhea for 5 days. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.32 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 114 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which part of her history best accounts for this blood gas?
opts: Aspirin
Salicylates are a toxin on the raised-gap list. Her gap is 9, normal, and her chloride is high. Tell: a normal gap with a high chloride points to bicarbonate loss, not aspirin.
competing diagnosis
Isoniazid
Isoniazid is a cause of raised-gap acidosis, which would push the gap above 12. Her gap is 9. Tell: with a normal gap, pick from the bicarbonate-loss causes.
competing diagnosis
Her diarrhea

Correct. Low pH and bicarbonate make a metabolic acidosis, and the gap is 138 - (15 + 114) = 9, normal, with a high chloride. Diarrhea, gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss, is one of the most common normal-gap causes. Metformin, aspirin and isoniazid all raise the gap.
Metformin
Metformin causes a raised-gap acidosis, with a gap above 12. Her gap is 9 with a high chloride. Tell: metformin sits on the raised-gap list.
competing diagnosis

set2.q: A 66-year-old man has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, hypertension treated with a thiazide, asthma treated with an inhaled bronchodilator, and kidney function that has worsened over a month. Serum ketones are negative. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.27 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 25 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 11 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Serum sodium 139 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 104 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 11 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which of his medicines should be stopped because it adds to this acidosis?
opts: No change to his medicines
Metformin is a listed raised-gap cause, and his gap is 24 with negative ketones. Leaving it in place keeps adding to the acidosis. Tell: when a raised-gap drug is on the list, stop it.
wrong stage or severity
Metformin

Correct. Low pH with a bicarbonate of 11 is a metabolic acidosis, and the gap is 139 - (11 + 104) = 24, well above 12. Metformin is on the raised-gap list, and stopping possible contributors is part of treating the underlying cause.
The thiazide
Diuretics cause a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, with a raised bicarbonate. His bicarbonate is 11. Tell: a thiazide pushes the pH up; it does not explain an acidosis.
reversed direction or value
The bronchodilator

An inhaled bronchodilator is not on any metabolic acidosis list, and it keeps his airways open. His gap of 24 points to a raised-gap cause. Tell: of his medicines, only metformin is a raised-gap cause.
adjacent fact

set2.q: A 77-year-old man with a urinary infection is hypotensive, with cool, mottled skin, and is breathing fast. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.43 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 22 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 139 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 101 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which process best explains his raised anion gap?
opts: Bicarbonate loss in diarrhea
Diarrhea gives a normal-gap acidosis with a high chloride. His gap is 24 with a normal chloride of 101. Tell: bicarbonate losses do not raise the gap; they raise chloride.
ruled out by a stated finding
Saline infusion

Saline causes a normal-gap, hyperchloremic acidosis. His gap is raised and his chloride is normal. Tell: saline and diarrhea are normal-gap causes; lactate, ketoacids, uremia and toxins raise the gap.
ruled out by a stated finding
Lactic acidosis from poor perfusion

Correct. Gap = 139 - (101 + 14) = 24, a raised-gap acidosis. Lactic acidosis from poor tissue perfusion is one of the big four raised-gap causes and fits his hypotension and mottling. His carbon dioxide of 22 is below the predicted 27 to 31 (1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29, plus or minus 2), a concurrent respiratory alkalosis of sepsis.
Hyperventilation from sepsis
Hyperventilation explains his concurrent respiratory alkalosis, but a respiratory disorder never produces a large anion gap. Tell: a gap of 24 needs an added acid such as lactate.
adjacent fact

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple and mixed acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
set2.q: A 73-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease takes a diuretic and has a potassium of 3.1 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.42 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 61 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45 mm Hg), bicarbonate 38 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 137 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 88 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). From a baseline carbon dioxide of 40 mm Hg and bicarbonate of 25 mEq/L, in chronic respiratory acidosis bicarbonate rises 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Give high-flow oxygen to lower carbon dioxide

In chronic respiratory acidosis oxygen is given carefully; a rapidly falling carbon dioxide can trigger alkalosis complications such as arrhythmias and seizures. Tell: chronic retainers get careful oxygen.
wrong stage or severity
Give sodium bicarbonate

Ingested alkali such as sodium bicarbonate is itself a cause of metabolic alkalosis, and her bicarbonate of 38 is already above the chronic prediction of about 32. Tell: alkali raises bicarbonate further, and hers is already high.
reversed direction or value
Make no change since her pH is normal

Her normal pH of 7.42 comes from two disorders offsetting each other, not from health; the diuretic is driving the alkalosis and her potassium is low. Tell: a normal pH with abnormal carbon dioxide and bicarbonate is a mixed disorder.
common lay belief
Stop the diuretic and replace potassium

Correct. Chronic compensation predicts bicarbonate = 25 + 3.5 x 2.1 = about 32; hers is 38, a metabolic alkalosis on top of chronic respiratory acidosis. Discontinuing contributors such as diuretics and treating potassium deficits are the listed steps for metabolic alkalosis.
